The Derg regime banned it and imprisoned players in Asmara, Addis Ababa and elsewhere. It was long associated with the wandering wata, the azmari and outlaws, the first begging with it and the last singing Fano war songs to it. Later, in Eritrea, it turned from an instrument once seen as a plaything into one of the most popular string instruments, entering secular music, love songs and poetry performance.

The krar (Krar) is a five- or six-string bowl lyre of Ethiopia and Eritrea, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.21. The body is often decorated with wood, cloth and beads, and it is tuned to a pentatonic scale; players sound it by bowing, plucking or strumming, plucking giving a soft timbre and strumming a pulsing harmony. A modern krar can be amplified like an electric guitar or a violin. It is common in secular music, love songs and poetry, and it is the usual instrument of the azmari or wata poet-musicians.
